title: Centralized Error Handling
learning_outcomes: Describe Custom application errors and explain how it relates to Centralized Error Handling.
Demonstrate Mapping errors to HTTP responses in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Avoiding duplicated handling.

content.intro: Centralized Error Handling is part of backend applications and web frameworks. This lesson connects Custom application errors, Mapping errors to HTTP responses, Avoiding duplicated handling to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: HTTP servers translate request method, URL, headers, and body into a response with a status, headers, and body. Exercise success, not-found, unsupported-method, invalid-body, oversized-body, and timeout scenarios.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: HTTP servers translate request method, URL, headers, and body into a response with a status, headers, and body. Validate method, path, content type, body size, and input; set appropriate status codes and close resources safely.

items.text: For Custom application errors, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Mapping errors to HTTP responses
items.text: HTTP methods, headers, status codes, and body formats form a contract. Handle malformed input, unsupported methods, and error responses explicitly.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Centralized Error Handling. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Custom application errors; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Mapping errors to HTTP responses, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting raw request bodies, returning success status for failures, or exposing files outside the intended root.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Create explicit routes, validate request data, centralize errors, and define timeouts and access rules.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
